The Binomial Distribution

Source: R/api-distributions.R
nv_binomial.Rd

Density (nv_dbinom), distribution function (nv_pbinom), and quantile function (nv_qbinom) for the Binomial distribution with parameters size and prob.

Usage

nv_dbinom(x, size, prob, log = FALSE)

nv_pbinom(q, size, prob, lower_tail = TRUE, log_p = FALSE)

nv_qbinom(p, size, prob, lower_tail = TRUE, log_p = FALSE)

Arguments

x, q

(arrayish)
Quantiles at which to evaluate the density (x) or the distribution function (q). These are counts, given as integers or floats.

size

(arrayish)
Number of trials, zero or more. Either a scalar, or an array of exactly the shape of x/q/p.

prob

(arrayish)
Probability of success on each trial, in \([0, 1]\), shaped like size.

log, log_p

(logical(1))
If TRUE, the densities/probabilities are given as logarithms. For nv_qbinom this describes the input p.

lower_tail

(logical(1))
If TRUE (default), probabilities are \(P(X \le x)\); otherwise, \(P(X > x)\).

p

(arrayish)
Probabilities at which to evaluate the quantile function. Values outside \([0, 1]\) give NaN. With log_p = TRUE, supply log-probabilities in \([-\infty, 0]\) instead.

Value

(arrayish)
nv_dbinom(), nv_pbinom(), and nv_qbinom() return an arrayish with the shape of x/q/p and the float data type described under Data Types.

Details

The Binomial distribution with size \(= n\) and prob \(= p\) has probability mass function: $$p(x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x}, \quad x = 0, \ldots, n$$ and zero elsewhere.

Invalid arguments give NaN, as in base R, but without a warning (that is prob outside \([0, 1]\), or a negative size).

nv_dbinom uses the saddle point expansion of Loader (2000), as base R does. nv_pbinom uses the incomplete beta function methods of DiDonato & Morris (1992) that base R's stats::pbeta() uses: a continued fraction, and an asymptotic expansion for large size near the mean. If the continued fraction has not converged after 1000 iterations, the result is NaN. nv_qbinom finds the smallest \(x\) with \(P(X \le x) \ge p\), starting from a Cornish-Fisher approximation as base R does.

Gradients

nv_dbinom can be differentiated with respect to prob, including at prob of 0 and 1. Where the density is zero there, as at prob = 0 for x > 0, the log-density is -Inf and has no derivative: it diverges. With log = TRUE the gradient returned there is zero, which is a convention of this implementation, not the mathematical derivative. nv_pbinom and nv_qbinom iterate until convergence in a nv_while() loop, so gradient() cannot differentiate them.

Data Types

nv_dbinom(), nv_pbinom() and nv_qbinom() compute at a float data type and return it. If x/q/p is a float, they compute at its data type; an R double settles on the default float. An integer x/q/p (an array or an R integer) is converted to the widest float among the arrays given for size or prob, or to the default float if there is none. Integers beyond \(2^{24}\) are not all exact at f32, so a large integer may change in that conversion.

An R value for size or prob takes the computing data type. An array is promoted to it, so a wider one (e.g. f64 for an f32 x) is an error.

References

Loader C (2000). “Fast and Accurate Computation of Binomial Probabilities.” https://www.r-project.org/doc/reports/CLoader-dbinom-2002.pdf.

DiDonato A, Morris A (1992). “Algorithm 708: Significant Digit Computation of the Incomplete Beta Function Ratios.” ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software, 18(3), 360–373. doi:10.1145/131766.131776 .

Dekker T (1971). “A floating-point technique for extending the available precision.” Numerische Mathematik, 18, 224–242. doi:10.1007/BF01397083 .

See also

nv_rbinom() for sampling from a Binomial distribution.

Examples

x <- nv_array(c(0, 1, 2, 5, 10))
nv_dbinom(x, size = 10, prob = 0.3)
#> AnvlArray
#>  2.8248e-02
#>  1.2106e-01
#>  2.3347e-01
#>  1.0292e-01
#>  5.9049e-06
#> [ CPUf32{5} ] 
nv_dbinom(x, size = 10, prob = 0.3, log = TRUE)
#> AnvlArray
#>   -3.5667
#>   -2.1115
#>   -1.4547
#>   -2.2738
#>  -12.0397
#> [ CPUf32{5} ] 

nv_pbinom(x, size = 10, prob = 0.3)
#> AnvlArray
#>  0.0282
#>  0.1493
#>  0.3828
#>  0.9527
#>  1.0000
#> [ CPUf32{5} ] 
nv_pbinom(x, size = 10, prob = 0.3, lower_tail = FALSE)
#> AnvlArray
#>  0.9718
#>  0.8507
#>  0.6172
#>  0.0473
#>  0.0000
#> [ CPUf32{5} ] 
nv_pbinom(x, size = 10, prob = 0.3, log_p = TRUE)
#> AnvlArray
#>  -3.5667
#>  -1.9017
#>  -0.9603
#>  -0.0485
#>   0.0000
#> [ CPUf32{5} ] 

p <- nv_array(c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
nv_qbinom(p, size = 10, prob = 0.3)
#> AnvlArray
#>  0
#>  3
#>  6
#> [ CPUf32{3} ] 
nv_qbinom(p, size = 10, prob = 0.3, lower_tail = FALSE)
#> AnvlArray
#>  6
#>  3
#>  0
#> [ CPUf32{3} ] 
nv_qbinom(nv_array(c(-700, -2, -0.1), dtype = "f64"), size = 1000, prob = 0.3, log_p = TRUE)
#> AnvlArray
#>    0
#>  284
#>  319
#> [ CPUf64{3} ]
